conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee. I’ll be part of your care team. You came in with high blood sugar and some symptoms—can you tell me what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, for about three days my blood sugar has been over 300. I haven’t missed any insulin doses. I’ve also had this dry cough for weeks, and lately my eyes have been stinging and tearing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Any fevers, nausea, or pain when you urinate?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No fevers or nausea. And no, I don’t have any UTI symptoms this time, even though I’ve had them before. I did miss my weekly fosfomycin dose last week, though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. We also saw you were in mild diabetic ketoacidosis—your blood sugar was 406 and your acid levels were off. We’ve started you on IV fluids and insulin to correct that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, that makes sense. I felt really weak and achy the day I came in. I knew something wasn’t right.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s common with DKA. We’re also checking your kidney function. Your creatinine was elevated at 1.9, which suggests some acute kidney injury, but it’s likely due to dehydration from high sugars.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I haven’t been eating much. My mom’s been in the hospital, and I’ve been stressed about my son too. I just haven’t had an appetite.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That stress and poor intake can definitely affect your blood sugar control. We’ll help you stabilize that. Your transplant team also checked your cyclosporine level—it was a bit low at 47, but we’ll keep monitoring it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I take it exactly as prescribed. Is that level concerning?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s slightly below the ideal range, but not dangerous. We’ll keep an eye on it. You’re still on your full immunosuppression—Cellcept, cyclosporine, and prednisone—all unchanged.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I don’t want any issues with my transplant.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re not seeing any signs of rejection. Your renal ultrasound was normal—no blockage or swelling in the kidney. Resistive indices actually improved a bit.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. What about my cough? My PCP thought it might be allergies from my car’s AC filter.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did a CT scan of your chest today. It shows stable changes from your past radiation—no signs of infection, pneumonia, or new lung issues. Your cough is likely due to allergies or postnasal drip.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So not an infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No. Your white blood cell count is normal, and we tested for viruses, Legionella, and BK virus—all negative. So it’s not a viral or bacterial infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s good. But my eyes still feel irritated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That could be related to the same allergies. We’re going to start you on a nasal spray—Nasacort—to help with the postnasal drip and eye symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was supposed to start fluticasone, but I never picked it up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nasacort is similar and should help. We’ll send it home with you—use two sprays in each nostril once daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your blood sugar is coming down—now 186—and your acid levels are improving. We’re transitioning you back to your insulin pump.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. Will the pump settings stay the same?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The endocrine team adjusted your basal rates slightly to help prevent future highs. For example, your morning rate is now a bit higher to cover dawn phenomenon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I can update that. What about my kidney numbers?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your creatinine dropped to 1.6—much better. It’s responding well to fluids. We expect it to keep improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs this morning look good. Glucose is 93, bicarbonate is normal, and creatinine is now 1.1. Your DKA has resolved.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a big improvement. Does that mean I can go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, likely tomorrow. Your cough and eye symptoms aren’t from infection, so we’re confident it’s safe to discharge you with the nasal spray.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my transplant is okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Your cyclosporine level this morning was 52—solidly in the target range. Keep taking all your immunosuppressants and Bactrim as prescribed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Should I restart my weekly fosfomycin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, continue it as before. It’s helping prevent UTIs, especially with your history and immunosuppression.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re finalizing your discharge plan. You’ll go home tomorrow. We just need to make sure you’re stable overnight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll need blood work in a few days—sodium, potassium, creatinine, and glucose. We’ll fax the order to your local lab. Also, follow up with your primary doctor and endocrinologist.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the pending tests—BK virus, strep antigen?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Those are still pending, but given your symptoms and clear CT, it’s unlikely they’ll change anything. Your doctor will review them at your follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Vital signs are stable, and you’ve been eating and drinking without issue. We’re clearing you for discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Keep using the Nasacort daily, monitor your blood sugar closely, and take all your medications. Call your doctor if you develop fever, shortness of breath, or high sugars again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And I’ll get that lab work done.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Dr. Lee.
